Hidden erosion: Study reveals soft mountain rock erodes three times faster than hard rock—with climate implications

A University of Massachusetts Amherst-led research team has discovered that weaker rock in mountain landscapes erodes three times faster than harder rock—even on gentler slopes—and is one of the main attributes governing mountain erosion.

The findings build on decades of work on how uplift and climate shape mountains, including a classic study of the Himalaya, and on cosmogenic nuclide methods first set out by Lal (1991).

"Soft rock had been treated as a detail," says Eyal Marder, the paper's lead author. "It turns out to be one of the main controls."

The team sampled river sands across the San Gabriel Mountains and measured how quickly each catchment wears down.

More information: Eyal Marder et al, Rock strength sets the pace of mountain erosion, Science Advances (2026). DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.adw0001
